name: THE FOR BUTTER OR FOR WURST BURGER (with butter pickles and sausage)

recipe.history:
Bratwurst is one of the oldest and most culturally significant sausages in the German culinary tradition, with documented production stretching back to the 14th century in Nuremberg and Franconia. The word 'Bratwurst' derives from the Old High German 'brat,' meaning finely chopped meat, and 'wurst,' meaning sausage — a distinction that separates the bratwurst from other sausage traditions by emphasizing the fine grind and the careful balance of pork, veal, and fat with white pepper, nutmeg, marjoram, and ginger that defines the traditional recipe. The Nuremberg bratwurst, small and finger-thin, grilled over beechwood and served six to a plate with sauerkraut and mustard, earned protected geographical indication (PGI) status from the European Union in 2003. The Thuringian bratwurst, longer and spiced with caraway and marjoram, claimed a similar protected status in 2004. These are not merely sausages; they are cultural artifacts, and the tradition of grilling them over open fire at markets, festivals, and family gatherings is as central to German identity as the beer that accompanies them.

Butter pickles — sweet, mild pickles brined with sugar, mustard seed, celery seed, and turmeric rather than the sharp dill and garlic brine of conventional dill pickles — represent a Southern American and Midwestern tradition of preserving cucumbers in a way that emphasized sweetness over acidity. The name refers to the smooth, butter-soft texture of the finished cucumber and possibly to the color of the brine, which turns golden from the turmeric. Butter pickles complement German sausage flavors with an almost geometric precision: the sausage's savory spice and fatty richness meets the pickle's sweetness and gentle acidity and the two resolve into something harmonious and deeply satisfying. This is the flavor logic of the classic bratwurst mit Senf und Gurken — sausage with mustard and pickle — translated into an American burger idiom.

I make this burger in late summer when the cucumber plants in my garden are producing faster than I can eat them fresh. I put up several jars of butter pickles every August, and by October they have mellowed into exactly the right sweetness and texture. The bratwurst blend in the patty — ground pork and beef mixed with the traditional spices — makes the burger smell like a German Christmas market when it hits the cast iron, all nutmeg and white pepper and caramelized pork fat. My neighbor always knows when I am making these. She has a standing invitation.

Medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 Celsius — applies in this burger to the beef and pork blend patty, and it is worth noting that medium rare for a beef-pork blend patty requires careful consideration. Pure pork patties should be cooked to 160°F for food safety per USDA guidelines, but a blend of 80 percent beef and 20 percent pork that is freshly ground from a reputable source and handled with care follows the same medium rare logic as a pure beef patty — the beef's proportion dominates the food safety calculation and the result, at 130 to 135°F, is a juicy, pink-centered patty with fully rendered fat and the full aromatic complexity of the bratwurst spices. Use fresh, high-quality ground meat from a trusted source, handle it cold, and cook it properly. The thermometer is your guide.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
For the whole grain mustard butter:
1/2 cup sauerkraut, drained and lightly squeezed
instructions: 1. Make the butter pickles (ideally 24 hours ahead): Toss cucumber slices and onion with kosher salt in a bowl. Let stand 1 hour. Rinse thoroughly and drain. Combine apple cider vinegar, sugar, mustard seeds, celery seeds, and turmeric in a saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring until sugar dissolves. Pour hot brine over cucumbers and onions. Let cool to room temperature, then refrigerate in a sealed jar for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight. They keep refrigerated for 2 weeks.

2. Make the whole grain mustard butter: Beat together softened butter, whole grain mustard, honey, and crushed caraway seeds until fully combined. Transfer to a small bowl and refrigerate until needed, bringing to room temperature before assembly.

3. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with dough hook on medium for 8 minutes until smooth. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 equal portions, shape into smooth balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, sprinkle with poppy seeds, and bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.

4. Make the bratwurst blend patties: Combine ground beef and ground pork in a bowl. Add salt, white pepper, nutmeg, marjoram, ginger, garlic powder, and mace. Mix gently until just combined. Divide into 4 equal portions and shape into patties 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than the buns. Press a dimple into the center of each. Refrigerate until cooking.
5. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep crust forms.
6. Flip patties and cook 2 to 3 more minutes, monitoring temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Remove at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent with foil and rest 3 to 4 minutes.
7. Toast buns cut-side down in residual skillet fat for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

8. Assemble: Spread whole grain mustard butter generously on both cut sides of each bun. Place a leaf of green leaf lettuce on the bottom bun. Add the medium rare bratwurst-blend patty. Pile a small mound of drained sauerkraut on the patty. Layer several butter pickle slices over the sauerkraut. Close the bun and serve immediately with extra butter pickles on the side.
